summary: Documents a process to apply architectural discipline to future development of the Session Initiation Protocol, responding to concerns that new features could harm security or add complexity. It sets out how proposals are reviewed. It was replaced by RFC 5727.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3427 explains how changes to SIP are supposed to happen. It says who decides what the protocol should do, who checks a proposal before it is discussed, and how a group that wants to try something out can do so without turning it into a standard.

questions: what is the sipping working group
subtitle: How a proposal to change SIP gets from an idea to a standard, and how experiments stay out of the way.

tldr.problem: SIP became popular enough that a continual flood of proposals arrived to extend it, and some of those proposals would have damaged the security of the protocol or made it much more complicated.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets out a two-stage process: the SIPPING working group filters requirements and the SIP working group owns the protocol and its extensions. It also defines a P- header prefix for experiments and private extensions, with seven conditions and IANA registration.
tldr.outcome: The memo was a Best Current Practice, and the RFC Editor index lists it as obsoleted by RFC 5727. It was later updated by RFC 3968 and RFC 3969.

facts.label: Working groups
facts.value: SIP owns the protocol, SIPPING filters the requirements

today: RFC 3427 is a December 2002 Best Current Practice, and the RFC Editor index lists it as obsoleted by RFC 5727. It was later updated by RFC 3968 and RFC 3969.

sections.title: Why SIP Needed a Change Process
sections.content:
The Session Initiation Protocol was originally developed for the initiation of multimedia sessions. Internet multimedia, voice over IP, IP telephony and SIP all became quite popular, both inside the IETF and with other standards groups, and the applications of SIP grew. One result of that popularity was a continual flood of suggestions for SIP modifications and extensions. The task for IETF management of SIP was to keep the protocol development focused on SIP's core strengths and the applications it does best.

The memo records the concern that motivated the process: that the addition of new SIP features can be damaging towards security, or can greatly increase the complexity of the protocol. The Transport Area directors, together with the chairs of the SIP and Session Initiation Proposal Investigation working groups, provided the suggestions for the changes and extensions set out here.

IETF working groups do not live forever, and mailing lists usually continue after a working group is concluded. If the SIP working group has closed and no suitable replacement is active, the Transport Area directors will use the non-working-group standards track document process described in the IETF standards process, using the SIP and SIPPING mailing lists and designated experts from the SIP community for advice. The IETF remains the home of extensions of SIP, and the requirement of standards track action remains as defined in the rest of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: SIP took off, and with it came a stream of ideas for changing it. Some of those ideas would have made the protocol harder to use or less safe, so the IETF wrote down how a proposal has to travel before it can change the protocol.

sections.title: The Two Working Groups
sections.content:
The IETF SIP working group has been chartered to be the owner of the SIP protocol, for as long as the working group exists. All changes or extensions to SIP must first exist as SIP working group documents, and the group is charged with being the guardian of the protocol for the Internet, so it should extend or change SIP only when there are compelling reasons to do so. Documents that must be handled by the SIP working group include new SIP methods, new SIP option tags, new response codes and new standards track SIP headers. With the exception of the P- headers described later, all SIP extensions must be standards track and must be developed in the IETF based upon requirements provided by the SIPPING working group.

The SIPPING working group is chartered as a filter in front of the SIP working group. It investigates requirements for applications of SIP, some of which may lead to requests for extensions, and the requirements may come from the community at large or from individuals reporting requirements determined by another standards body. The SIPPING working group may determine that the requirements can be satisfied by SIP without modifications, that they are not sufficiently general to warrant a change to SIP, that they justify a change to SIP, or that they should be combined with other requirements to solve a more general problem or the same problem in a more flexible way.

Because SIP gets so much attention, some application designers may want to use it just because it is there, such as for controlling household appliances. SIPPING should act as a filter, accepting only requirements that play to the best strengths of SIP, such as real-time presence. When the SIPPING working group decides on a set of requirements, it forwards them to the SIP working group, and it may also document usage or applications of SIP that need no protocol extensions.

It is appropriate for any working group to develop SIP event packages, but the working group must have charter approval to do so. The IETF also requires an individual RFC publication for the registration of event packages developed outside the scope of an IETF working group.
sections.plainLanguage: Two groups share the job. One collects what people actually need, and throws away the requests that do not suit SIP. The other owns the protocol itself and decides what to add to it.

sections.title: The Change Process
sections.content:
Anyone who thinks that the existing SIP protocol is applicable to their application, yet not sufficient for the task, must write an individual Internet-Draft explaining the problem they are trying to solve, why SIP is the applicable protocol, and why the existing protocol will not work. The draft must include a detailed set of requirements, distinct from solutions, that SIP would need to meet, and it must describe in detail any security issues that arise from meeting those requirements. After it is published, the authors should send a note to the SIPPING mailing list to start the discussion.

The SIPPING chairs, together with the Transport Area Directors, decide whether the problems raised warrant being added to the SIPPING charter, based on the mailing list discussion, and they consider whether the requirements can be merged with other requirements from other applications and refine the draft accordingly. If the chairs and the Area Directors agree, the Area Directors present the proposed charter modifications to the IESG and IAB in the usual way, and if the IESG, with IAB advice, approves the charter changes, the SIPPING working group can work on the problems described in the draft.

In a separate Internet-Draft, the authors may describe a set of changes to SIP that would meet the requirements, and that draft is then passed to the SIP working group for consideration if it is warranted. The SIP working group is not required to adopt the proposed solution. The SIPPING working group may also evaluate proposals for extensions that suit SIP but are not sufficiently general for standards track activity, and will try to determine whether the new proposal meets the requirements for publication as a P- header within a specific scope of applicability.

The Transport Area Directors may, case by case, support a process in which the requirements analysis is implicit and the SIP working group requests the addition of a charter item without a full SIPPING process, and the memo says this will be the exception. The result of all this is that SIP extensions come only from the IETF, the body that created SIP, and the IETF will not publish a SIP extension RFC outside the processes described. The SIP working group is required to protect the architectural integrity of SIP and must not add features that do not have general use beyond the specific case, nor add features just to make a particular function more efficient at the expense of simplicity or robustness.
sections.plainLanguage: Start with a draft that states the problem and the requirements, without proposing a fix. The filter group decides whether the problem is worth solving in SIP at all, and the group that owns the protocol decides what to do about it.

sections.title: P-Headers for Experiments and Private Use
sections.content:
In an idealised protocol model, extensible design would be self-contained, and new extensions would naturally have an architectural coherence with the original protocol. That vision has not been attained in standards track protocols. Interoperability problems can be addressed by capability negotiation rules, but the effects of adding features that overlap, or that deal with a point solution and are not general, are much harder to control with rules. The Transport Area therefore calls for architectural guardianship and the application of Occam's razor by the SIP working group.

Following the IETF tradition of running code and rough consensus, it is valid to allow the development of SIP extensions that are either not ready for standards track but might be understood for that role after some running code, or are private or proprietary in nature, because a characteristic motivating them is usage that is known not to fit the Internet architecture for SIP. These are called P- headers, for preliminary, private or proprietary. Two key issues have to be considered: clearly indicating the unarchitected or not yet understood nature of the extension, and preventing identity conflicts between extensions.

An informational SIP header can be registered as a P- header if all of seven conditions are met. A designated expert must review the proposal for applicability to SIP and conformance to the guidelines, and the reviewer may cite the guidelines that have not been followed. The proposed extension must not define SIP option tags, response codes or methods, and its function must not overlap with current or planned chartered extensions. It must be of a purely informational nature and must not significantly change the behaviour of SIP entities that support it, where headers that merely provide additional information pertinent to a request or a response are acceptable, and headers that redefine or contradict normative behaviour are what is meant by significantly different behaviour. It must not undermine SIP security in any sense, and the draft must address security issues in detail as if it were a standards track document, although where the intended application scenario makes assumptions about security, the security considerations only need to meet that scenario, and in any case security issues need to be discussed for arbitrary usage scenarios including the general Internet case. It must be clearly documented in an individual or working group informational RFC and registered with IANA, and the RFC must carry an applicability statement that documents the useful scope of the proposal and explains its limitations and why it is not suitable for general use of SIP on the Internet.

Any implementation of a P- header must include the P- prefix on the header name. P- extensions are not IETF standards of any kind and must not be required by any production deployment considered compliant to IETF specifications: an implementation is only SIP compliant if it falls back to baseline behaviour when it ignores all P- headers, and if, when using P- headers, it does not contradict any normative behaviour. To prevent identity conflicts, the document provides an IANA process to register the P- headers, and the handling of unknown P- headers is to ignore them. Any P- header used outside of a very restricted research or teaching environment must meet the requirements and must be documented in an RFC and be IANA registered, and IANA registration is permitted when the IESG approves the draft.
sections.plainLanguage: If you want to try something out before the IETF agrees on it, you can, but you must say so in the name. A P- header is not a standard, nobody is allowed to require one, and it has to be registered so two people do not pick the same name.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo's security argument is short and direct. Complexity and indeterminate or hard to define protocol behaviour, depending on which of many extensions operate, is a fine breeding ground for security flaws. That is the reason the process insists on a requirements draft that states the security issues in detail, and on the rule that extensions must not undermine SIP security in any sense.

All Internet-Drafts that present new requirements for SIP must include a discussion of the security requirements and implications inherent in the proposal. All RFCs that modify or extend SIP must show that they have adequate security and do not worsen SIP's existing security considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: The more extensions there are, the harder it is to reason about what a protocol will do, and that is where security bugs come from. So every proposal has to say what its security consequences are, and every extension has to show that it does not make things worse.

sections.title: Registration and Naming Rules
sections.content:
The SIP specification directs IANA to establish registries for SIP method names, SIP option tags and SIP response codes, and to amend the practices used for the existing registry for SIP headers. With the exception of P- headers, entries go into these registries only by approval of an Internet-Draft as a standards track RFC. Each RFC must include an IANA considerations section, and registration is done at the time the IESG announces its approval of the draft that carries the registration requests.

The naming rules keep the two worlds apart. Standard headers and messages must not begin with the leading characters P-, and P- header names must begin with them. No P- header that would conflict with an existing standards track header without the P- prefix is allowed. Each registration of a P- header also reserves the name of the header as it would appear without the prefix, although that reserved name does not appear in the registry and only appears if a later standards track document uses it. The reserved standard name must not be used in a SIP implementation before the header is standardised. Short forms of headers must only be assigned to standards track headers, so P- headers must not have short forms.

The event notification specification directs IANA to establish a registry for SIP event packages and SIP event template packages. For event template packages, entries go into the registry only by approval of a draft for a standards track RFC; for ordinary event packages, entries go in only by approval of a draft for an RFC of any type. In either case the IESG announcement of approval authorises the registration.
sections.plainLanguage: Method names, option tags, response codes and standard headers are registered only when the protocol goes standards track. P- headers are registered differently, and their names are reserved so that a later standard cannot collide with them.

messages.label: REQUIREMENTS DRAFT
messages.note: An Internet-Draft stating the problem, why SIP applies, the requirements and the security issues.

messages.label: CHARTER REQUEST
messages.note: The chairs and Area Directors ask for the charter to be widened.

messages.label: CHARTER APPROVED
messages.note: With IAB advice, the IESG approves the charter change.

messages.label: REQUIREMENTS
messages.note: The agreed requirements are forwarded to the group that owns the protocol.

messages.label: SOLUTION DRAFT
messages.note: A separate Internet-Draft describing changes that would meet the requirements.

messages.label: WORKING GROUP DECISION
messages.note: The working group is not required to adopt the proposed solution.

viz.caption: THE SEVEN CONDITIONS FOR A P- HEADER

items.title: Expert review
items.text: A designated expert must review the proposal for applicability and conformance.

items.title: No new protocol parts
items.text: It must not define option tags, response codes or methods.

items.title: No overlap
items.text: Its function must not overlap with current or planned chartered extensions.

items.title: Informational only
items.text: It must not significantly change the behaviour of SIP entities that support it.

items.title: No harm to security
items.text: It must not undermine SIP security, and the draft must discuss security in detail.

items.title: Documented and registered
items.text: It must be in an Informational RFC and registered with IANA.

items.title: Scope stated
items.text: The RFC must say where it is useful and why it is not for general use.
